summary: Ron DeSantis is Florida’s Republican governor, whose 2019–2026 administration used state executive power to reshape school choice and higher education, build immigration enforcement partnerships, regulate a major corporate special district, strengthen anti-boycott-of-Israel policies and advance new congressional maps. After declining to take sides in the August 2026 Republican primary to succeed him, DeSantis endorsed Byron Donalds for the general election despite prior public disagreements, while James Fishback, Jay Collins and Paul Renner each represented a different claim to the DeSantis legacy.

chapters.title: From congressional conservative to Florida executive
chapters.dek: Ron DeSantis is Florida’s Republican governor, whose 2019–2026 administration used state executive power to reshape school choice and higher education, build immigration enforcement partnerships, regulate a major corporate special district, strengthen anti-boycott-of-Israel policies and advance new congressional maps. After declining to take sides in the August 2026 Republican primary to succeed him, DeSantis endorsed Byron Donalds for the general election despite prior public disagreements, while James Fishback, Jay Collins and Paul Renner each represented a different claim to the DeSantis legacy.
chapters.body:
DeSantis entered Florida state politics as an ex-Navy judge advocate and congressman, serving the Daytona Beach-area 6th district from 2013 to 2018. He narrowly defeated Democrat Andrew Gillum in 2018 and became the state’s 46th governor in January 2019. His 2022 reelection against Charlie Crist was considerably less competitive: official returns give the incumbent 4,614,210 votes, or 59.4%, versus Crist’s 3,106,313, or 40.0%. [[RD01,RD02,RD03,RD04,RD05]]

His 2023 presidential launch tried to translate Florida executive results into a national Republican agenda, but he suspended his bid on January 21, 2024. This divide between state-level organizational control and national primary success is important when evaluating his role in Florida’s 2026 gubernatorial succession: governorship, fundraising, and high-profile executive orders did not in themselves prove national electoral viability. [[RD05,RD40]]

chapters.title: COVID governance and the theory of executive restraint
chapters.body:
DeSantis’s COVID response changed over time: Florida initially issued health emergency actions, then in September 2020 reopened businesses and narrowed local authority to fine people for mask noncompliance. Supporters presented this as economic liberty and resistance to prolonged restrictions. Public-health critics argued it risked spread while infections continued. This dossier records the decision and controversy, without claiming a causal mortality ranking absent adjusted epidemiological evidence. [[RD06]]

This experience became a governing precedent for more activist executive action in other domains: rejecting central control over businesses in the pandemic coexisted with far more intervention against corporations, university boards, and local governments later. The contrast is ideological and institutional, not automatically a legal inconsistency. [[RD06,RD08,RD24,RD51]]

chapters.title: Education: parental authority, school choice, and higher education
chapters.body:
HB1557, signed March 28, 2022, constrained classroom instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in early grades and required specified parental involvement and notification. The legislative text as originally signed matters: later administrative rules or subsequent changes should never be backdated to 2022. HB7, signed the following month, sought to restrict specified compelled teachings about race and sex across public education and workplaces; the 11th Circuit later held the private-employer speech restriction unconstitutional. [[RD07,RD08,RD09]]

In 2023 the governor signed HB1, expanding scholarship eligibility for Florida school choice and removing previous income requirements, with prioritization rules still applicable. On May 15 he signed SB266, which restricted spending on DEI in public higher education and paired institutional ideology reform with workforce-oriented policy. These were actual laws, not merely campaign promises, but comparative education outcome claims require independent measures. [[RD10,RD11,RD12]]

chapters.title: Immigration: from employment checks to state-federal architecture
chapters.body:
SB1718 (2023) increased Florida’s involvement in immigration-related employment, transportation and public-sector data systems. The required E-Verify population was private employers with at least 25 employees, not all employers, and hospital status collection did not itself abolish emergency-treatment obligations. These distinctions matter for any Worldview eligibility or process flow chart. [[RD13,RD14]]

DeSantis’s January 2025 special-session proposal sought extensive enforcement changes; he ultimately backed the negotiated SB2-C enacted in February. The final statute appropriated roughly $298.83 million and established a State Board of Immigration Enforcement and other state mechanisms. He then sought federal 287(g) agreements for state agencies, meaning trained state officers exercise specified delegated federal functions under federal oversight. [[RD15,RD16,RD17,RD18,RD19]]

By July 2026 reporting based on Florida law-enforcement data, 272 of 394 agencies had active 287(g) task-force agreements, but signing an agreement is not synonymous with training, arrest or removal. Government releases citing thousands of arrests in Operation Tidal Wave and new Alligator Alcatraz detention capacity are evidence of executive claims; an accurate profile requires adjudication, detention, deportation, cost, complaint, and judicial outcome records before drawing operational success conclusions. [[RD20,RD21,RD22,RD23]]

chapters.title: Corporations and civil society: Disney, local order, institutions
chapters.body:
DeSantis’s conflict with Walt Disney World turned into law through HB9-B in February 2023, restructuring the Reedy Creek district and appointing a state control board. Disney said it was being punished for opposing state education policy; DeSantis said ending special privileges was fair corporate governance. A federal lawsuit was dismissed in January 2024, while a development-governance dispute was settled that March. Neither outcome alone proves all rhetorical allegations about retaliatory intent. [[RD24,RD25,RD26]]

Broader state-power examples include HB1365 in 2024, addressing unauthorized public camping and giving residents and businesses a tool to sue noncompliant local governments. Its legislative summary specifies civil mechanisms rather than establishing a new penalty for every person sleeping outside. DeSantis has also promoted property insurance and taxation changes, but the impact of those reforms should not be measured solely by the governor’s announcements. [[RD55,RD54,RD59]]

chapters.title: Israel policy: state power, education law and public alignment
chapters.body:
DeSantis has made support for Israel unusually central to Florida executive action: a ceremonial state cabinet meeting at the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem in May 2019, HB741 protections for religion in public K-20 education that month, another antisemitism-related law (HB269) signed during an April 2023 Israel visit, and a highly explicit pro-Israel statement following the October 7 Hamas attacks. The state actions and the candidate’s statements are separately documented. [[RD27,RD28,RD29,RD30,RD31]]

Florida’s 2025 SB1678 broadened investment and other state restrictions on entities that boycott Israel, including academic boycotts. Criticism of Israeli government policy, harassment prohibited by particular laws, investment screening and academic free-speech protections are different legal categories; the legislation should be summarized by its operative text. Miami-Dade County’s announced purchase of an additional $25m in Israel Bonds in October 2023 belongs to county administration and must not be recorded as a direct DeSantis purchase. [[RD32,RD33,RD60]]

The State University System’s October 2023 directive concerning Students for Justice in Palestine chapters was challenged as a speech violation. Court proceedings resulted in dismissal for standing/no imminent injury, not a merits ruling that government is free to eliminate political student organizations for protected speech. Retain the chancellor’s conduct, DeSantis consultation, and litigants’ allegations as distinct records. [[RD34,RD35]]

chapters.title: Elections and institutional power: the 2026 congressional map
chapters.body:
DeSantis called a 2026 special session to redraw Florida’s congressional boundaries between censuses; his office submitted an executive-drafted plan. The legislature passed HB1-D in April and he signed it May 4, 2026. This is one of the clearest practical examples of his preference for deploying state political machinery to pursue policy and electoral objectives. [[RD50,RD51,RD52]]

The 2026 congressional plan was promptly contested under Florida constitutional rules. A trial court denied a preliminary injunction, and judicial proceedings remained live in the available August 2026 case tracker. A validly enacted map and an ultimately constitutional map are not identical findings; pending claims must be marked unresolved. [[RD53]]

chapters.title: Presidential money, state PACs and the attribution problem
chapters.body:
Three different types of financial entities should not be combined: Florida state candidate/committee accounts, DeSantis’s 2024 federal presidential infrastructure, and federal super/hybrid PACs. The 2022 Florida political committee once called Friends of Ron DeSantis later appears as Empower Parents PAC in secondary public indexes. The aggregator’s $164.2m 2022 contribution figure is a lead requiring reconciliation to raw Florida reporting, not a verified all-in donor total for DeSantis personally. [[RD36,RD37]]

FEC records identify Restore Our Nation (RON PAC), C00841130, as a hybrid PAC with $2,884,109.25 receipts from Jan 1, 2025 to Sep 30, 2026 and $1,169,659.51 in disbursements in the same period. Never Back Down (C00834077) is a separate independent expenditure-only Super PAC. DeSantis’s FEC candidate page cautions that an authorized presidential committee was later converted to PAC status. Entity IDs, time periods, authorized status and transfers must be reconciled before calculating donor influence. [[RD38,RD39,RD40]]

chapters.title: Successor politics: Collins, Renner, Fishback and Donalds
chapters.body:
DeSantis appointed Jay Collins lieutenant governor in August 2025, giving Collins a real working relationship and positioning him publicly as a potential successor. Paul Renner was a former legislative partner, especially in the 2023 school-choice program, while Fishback campaigned as an admirer of DeSantis’s model of government. These are three distinct kinds of connection: appointment, legislative collaboration and one-sided public praise. None is equivalent to a documented 2026 primary endorsement. [[RD41,RD42,RD11,RD47]]

In June 2026 DeSantis publicly favored a GOP candidate debate while the Republican Party of Florida declined to stage a full debate and then rescinded Fishback’s invitation to party programming. The party’s stated rationale was Fishback’s decision to participate in a rival unsanctioned event. DeSantis’s position and party officials’ action should not be collapsed into a single actor’s decision. [[RD43,RD44,RD62]]

On August 6 he declined to endorse any of the GOP primary candidates despite praising Renner’s governing potential. After Donalds won the August primary, DeSantis endorsed the entire GOP statewide ticket at the September 1 party forum, including Donalds, despite earlier disputes over Black history standards and political credit. The accurate relationship record is therefore: public disagreement, neutral primary, post-primary partisan endorsement. [[RD45,RD46,RD47,RD48,RD49]]

chapters.title: 2026 priorities and unresolved legacy
chapters.body:
In October 2026 DeSantis campaigned for proposed Amendment 3, a property-tax-relief constitutional amendment to expand homestead exemptions on non-school taxes. His office projected substantial eventual homeowner savings. These are stated policy aims and modeled effects, not a passed amendment or realized savings as of the October 28 research cutoff. [[RD59]]

The DeSantis legacy is consequently best evaluated as a set of discrete institutional experiments: aggressive immigration delegation, restrictions and choice in education, state intervention against concentrated corporate privilege, explicit alignment with Israel, mid-decade mapmaking and fiscal reforms. Supporters regard these as proof that a governor can execute conservative policy; critics point to speech rights, legal challenges, minority representation, detention practices and affordability. Worldview should keep enactments, judicial outcomes, public claims and measurable effects in separate, linked records. [[RD09,RD17,RD20,RD23,RD24,RD33,RD34,RD53,RD54,RD59]]
